paras: The Albany Elk pin incident was a confrontation in Albany, Georgia, in late 1903 in which about ten white men made a Black member of the touring Black Patti Troubadours remove his Elk pin. No one was reported hurt, but the men had knives drawn when they began to cut the pin from his coat. The Indianapolis Freeman printed the account under the head "A Georgia Absurdity."

The Black Patti Troubadours were touring Georgia, Florida and Virginia in the autumn of 1903. Several members, including the Freeman's correspondent, had joined a Norfolk, Virginia, lodge of the I.B.P.O. Elks, and the correspondent wrote that the whole company were "colored Elks."

According to the correspondent, it happened on "Wednesday last" during the company's engagement at the Sale-Davis opera house. Company members wearing Elk buttons on the street "created a little sensation," and later that day "a mob of about ten white men" stopped one of them and asked what he was doing with the pin. He said he had a right to wear it, and when their spokesman said he had his card, he answered that he had his also.

After a consultation and an examination of his card, the spokesman said, "you niggers can't wear them pins in this town, and you've got to take 'em off." When they began to cut the pin from his coat with knives drawn, he refused to let them and took it out himself.

After hearing the story, the correspondent removed his own pin; an Albany cafe proprietor then told him that about three years earlier a white uniformed rank there had disbanded after a Black Knights of Pythias rank from Brunswick paraded in the same regalia. No report of arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The only account found ran in the company's correspondence column in the Indianapolis Freeman of 14 November 1903, among notes on initiations and banquets. The Freeman called it "a peculiar incident" and closed with the story of white lodgemen who would rather disband than share regalia with Black men. No white-press report was found.
